<reflection>
- One iteration has already been completed, and we now have the first fitting results.
- The current result set is highly non-discriminating: many mechanisms cluster within about 1 NLL unit of the best model. Only M20 is clearly disfavored, while M3, M14, and M18 are somewhat weaker but still not decisively excluded.
- The best current fit is M7, but M17, M12, M8, M6, M11, M2, M10, M1, and M15 remain very plausible. So it would be premature to focus narrowly on M7 versus one runner-up.
- The first experiment used added product and moderate catalyst; this likely compressed differences among several reversible and deactivation models. To make progress, the next experiment should probe a different mechanistic axis rather than repeating product-perturbed conditions.
- My aim this turn is to discriminate broadly among remaining plausible mechanisms by emphasizing catalyst-order and substrate-order effects while removing the confounding effect of initial product. This aim is achieved by moving to high catalyst, low-to-moderate substrate, and zero added product.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
The remaining plausible mechanisms fall into several broad classes:

1. Simple single-catalyst turnover and close variants:
- M1, M10, M15 are effectively tied.
- These should show fairly regular kinetics with no strong dependence on added product beyond reversible effects already tested.

2. Catalyst activation / latent active species:
- M6 and M8 remain strongly plausible.
- These can produce induction behavior or altered effective catalyst order, especially when catalyst is relatively abundant and no product is initially present.

3. Substrate-assisted or higher substrate-occupancy pathways:
- M7 is currently best.
- M5, M16, M19, and to some degree M14/M18 relate to catalyst-substrate-complex-dependent branching.
- These are often more visible when catalyst is sufficiently high that catS builds rapidly, while substrate is not so overwhelming that all mechanisms appear similarly pseudo-first-order.

4. Product- or substrate-dependent deactivation:
- M11, M12, M17 remain competitive.
- Since the prior run included added product, product-associated mechanisms may have fit well simply because that condition created immediate sensitivity.
- A zero-product run is therefore valuable to see whether those models still explain the data well when product accumulates only endogenously.

5. Catalyst aggregation / dimerization:
- M2 remains plausible; M3 is weaker but not dead.
- Aggregation effects become much more pronounced at elevated catalyst concentration.
- Comparing high-cat behavior against prior moderate-cat behavior should reveal whether catalyst order is anomalous.

A broadly discriminating design should therefore:
- eliminate initial product to remove one source of degeneracy among reversible/product-sensitive models,
- raise catalyst substantially to magnify catalyst-catalyst interaction, activation, and deactivation signatures,
- keep substrate on the lower side of moderate so that catalyst is not trivially limiting and the system can explore free-cat, catS, and possibly higher-order catalyst regimes during the run.

Why this helps many mechanisms at once:
- M2/M3/M13-like catalyst-coupled processes become more distinct at high catalyst.
- M6/M8 activation mechanisms may display altered initial transients or acceleration relative to simple M1.
- M7/M16/M19 substrate-complex pathways will respond differently when catalyst is abundant and substrate is not saturating.
- M11/M12/M17 deactivation channels become distinguishable by when and how rate decays emerge without exogenous product.
- M1/M10/M15 serve as baseline simpler behaviors under the new regime.

This is preferable to an extreme high-substrate design, which could mask differences by driving near-complete catalyst saturation, and preferable to very low catalyst, which would suppress higher-order catalyst effects. The proposed condition is thus a balanced but strategically shifted regime aimed at reducing uncertainty across the whole plausible set.
</hypothesis>
